newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durable goods orders weaken unexpectedly in May.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durable goods orders weaken unexpectedly in May.

text.p: Orders for costly manufactured goods weakened unexpectedly in May, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday, partly because of a drop in demand for commercial aircraft and for new cars and parts.

New orders for durable goods fell 0.6 percent last month to a seasonally adjusted $176.1 billion, contrary to Wall Street economists' forecasts of a 0.6 percent increase. Shipments of finished goods dropped for the first time this year and order backlogs were flat in May.
The falloff in orders during May was relatively broad-based, with most major categories of manufactured goods aside from electronic and electrical products showing a decline from April.
It followed a revised 1.8 percent jump in orders during April that previously was reported as a smaller 1.3 percent increase.
Weaker May orders for manufactured goods appeared to fit with other signs that economic growth was slowing in the second quarter after booming ahead at a 5.8 percent annual rate in the first quarter.

Orders for durable goods, items like cars and home appliances that are intended to last at least three years, can indicate the future strength of the manufacturing sector, which in turn weighs heavily on the overall economy.

Transportation orders declined 3.3 percent in May to $38.4 billion after a 2.8 percent April rise. It was the third decline in transportation orders in the past four months and the department said it was due to declines for both motor vehicles and parts and for aircraft and parts.
Transportation goods account for more than one-fifth of total monthly durable goods orders, so swings in demand strongly affect the overall figure.
Excluding transportation, durables orders were up a slim 0.2 percent in May after a 1.6 percent April increase.

On Tuesday, the head of the regional Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Robert Parry, said he thought the economy had slowed in the second quarter. He said that "surprisingly favourable" developments had kept inflation in check but added that the potential for resurgent prices remains a concern.
Parry is a voting member of the Federal Reserve's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, which meets July 1-2 to plot interest-rate strategy.
Orders for defence goods, which experience wide monthly swings, fell 12.8 percent last month to $5.5 billion after a 27.5 percent increase in April.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, an indication of business investment in new equipment, were up 0.7 percent to $44 billion last month after falling 1.7 percent in April.

Shipments of durable goods, an indication of current demand, fell 1.2 percent in May after rising 1.3 percent in April. It was the first month since last December that fewer finished products left the factory gate.
Unfilled orders were flat last month after two straight monthly declines, down 0.3 percent in April and off 0.5 percent in March.

Orders for electronic and electrical goods increased by 10.4 percent to $30.8 billion after a 3.2 percent April drop. The department said stronger demand for communications equipment and for electronic componments accounted for the May orders pickup.

Orders for industrial machinery, which includes computers, decreased 1 percent in May to $33.5 billion after a 2.9 percent April rise. Orders for primary metals were down 2.4 percent to $15.5 billion following a 2.3 percent gain in April.
